t1-2.what:
Definition: In a design interview, just mentioning "controlled vs uncontrolled" is not enough — support both. The production component standard is: if the value prop is provided, it is controlled; if not, the component keeps its own state (starting from defaultValue).

This pattern exists in every good library — Radix, MUI, React Aria, etc.
t1-2.analogy: Car's cruise control. If you want, press the accelerator yourself (controlled); if you want, the car maintains its speed on its own (uncontrolled). Both options should be available — providing only one is a stubborn design.
t1-2.why:
In 90% of use cases, the user doesn't care about the value — they just need a working dropdown. Forcing those 90% to be controlled means unnecessary useState everywhere. But the remaining 10% (when using a form library, or syncing the value with the URL) definitely need control.

The hybrid pattern satisfies both — and by writing a useControllableState hook, it can be reused across the entire design system.
pros: Simple case stays simple, complex case is possible
A single hook reused across the entire design system
onChange fires in both modes — analytics/validation works
cons: A bit of extra code in each component
Bugs can appear if the mode switches mid-flight
You have to explain the reasoning for both branches to the interviewer
gotchas: If a value appears from undefined, it means an uncontrolled-to-controlled switch — always add a dev warning
onChange should also be called in uncontrolled mode, otherwise the consumer will be left blind
Do NOT update internal state in controlled mode — otherwise you have two sources of truth
terms: value comes from the parent’s state
the component maintains its own value
supports both — if a value is provided it’s controlled, otherwise internal

console.warn('Select controlled/uncontrolled ke beech switch ho gaya');

t1-4.what:
Definition: There are two ways to provide flexibility:

  • Configuration — <Card title icon actions showBorder />. Simple, but each new case needs a new prop.
  • Composition — <Card><Card.Header/><Card.Body/></Card>. More code to write, but unlimited flexibility.

The middle path: slots — <Card header={<X/>} footer={<Y/>} />.
t1-4.why:
Rule of thumb that works in interviews: "Config for data, composition for structure." Anything that is data (title text, disabled) remains a prop. Anything that is structure (where and how it appears) should come from children or a slot.

Bonus that people often forget: composition also provides a performance benefit — children are created outside the parent, so when the parent’s state changes their element reference stays the same and React skips rendering them.
pros: No new prop needed for a new requirement
Composition gives a free performance benefit
Component code stays small
cons: Call site becomes verbose
Structure is not enforced — user can put anything
Simple cases may feel over-engineered
gotchas: Saying "config for data, composition for structure" in an interview impresses everyone
Slots (ReactNode props) are the middle path — fixed structure with flexible content
Be sure to mention the performance benefit of children as props — very few people know this
terms: building a larger component by combining small pieces
describing everything about a component via props
named prop that receives JSX — header, footer, actions
where: separating the wrapper’s state from a heavy child

// SLOTS -- the middle path, structure is fixed while content is flexible
// perf bonus -- Heavy parent ke render se azaad
// perf bonus -- independent of the Heavy parent's render

t1-1.what:
Definition: Component API design means defining the component’s public contract: which props, what names, which are required, which have defaults, and what not to provide.

In the design round the interviewer asks first — "What will its API be?" Your answer should not be a list of props, but a thought: which data is essential, which is optional, and where the user needs control.
t1-1.analogy: The restaurant menu. A small menu = every dish turns out well. A 200-item menu = the kitchen gets confused, quality suffers. A component is the same — a small, clean API is more reliable.
t1-1.why:
Once an API is public, changing it is a breaking change. In a design system, renaming a prop means refactoring 200 files. That’s why interviewers look to see if you think ahead.

The most common mistake: adding a new boolean prop for every new requirement — isBig, isRed, hasIcon, showBorder. After 6 months you have 22 props and no combination makes sense. The solution is variant + composition.
pros: Union variant prevents impossible combinations from being created
...rest passes native props through for free
Small API = fewer breaking changes, fewer docs
cons: In the variant approach, cases with only a "tiny difference" are difficult
Providing an escape hatch (className) can break the design system’s consistency
Learning composition takes time — props feel more obvious
gotchas: In the design round, state the API first, implementation later — the interviewer is waiting for that
Place the ...rest spread ... after (or before) your own props — decide deliberately which wins
Use a boolean prop only when it is truly binary — for three states use a string union
terms: all the props of a component that external users use
a prop that lets the user step outside the default behavior (className, render)
adding a new prop for every new requirement — a component with 20 props
where: Button, Input, Card — which 100 people will use
the answer to "What will its API be?" comes from here

// ...rest is ESSENTIAL -- aria-*, data-*, onFocus all pass through
SAHI -- union variants + composition + escape hatch
CORRECT -- union variants + composition + escape hatch

t1-3.what:
Definition: It holds a parent state and provides it to its children via Context. The user writes it like HTML — <Tabs><Tabs.List><Tabs.Tab/></Tabs.List><Tabs.Panel/></Tabs>.

In a design round this is the answer to flexibility — when the interviewer asks "what if the client wants a divider between tabs?"
t1-3.why:
The config-object API (<Tabs items={[...]} />) is fine as long as the layout is fixed. As soon as the first custom requirement arrives — "badge with tab", "divider", "tabs at the bottom" — you have to add a new prop. In a compound component the layout belongs to the user, you only provide the behaviour (state, keyboard, ARIA).

That is why Radix/Headless UI are all compound — they provide behaviour, not look.
pros: Full layout control is with the user
Prop explosion ends
Behaviour (keyboard, ARIA) in one place — free for every consumer
cons: Implicit dependency — runtime error if used in the wrong place
Too much boilerplate for small widgets
Dot-notation types in TypeScript require a bit of extra work

Don't inspect children with React.Children.map — it breaks as soon as a nested wrapper appears
Memoize the Context value with useMemo otherwise all tabs re-render on every render
terms: multiple components that together form a widget
parent state that children automatically receive via Context
the place where the user can insert their content

t1-5.what:
Definition: Keep the state only as high as necessary — no more than one level. Default is at the bottom; lift it up only when both siblings need it.

In the design round this is the first answer for performance — before memo.
t1-5.analogy: Household items. Keep the tea cup in the kitchen, not in the storage room. Anything that is used only in one room, placing it in a common area causes trouble for everyone.
t1-5.why:
The higher the state, the larger the subtree that will re-render on update. If a modal’s isOpen is in App, opening the modal causes the entire app to render. Keeping that state in Modal means only the modal re-renders.

In an interview say: "first I push the state down, memo is the last resort" — because memo has its own cost, while colocation is free.
pros: Zero-cost optimization — no memo, no library
Component becomes portable — can be moved anywhere
Code is easy to read — state is next to its use
cons: If you later need it in two places you have to lift it
Prop drilling can increase in deep trees
Does not work for global things (auth, theme)
gotchas: Put filter, tab, page, search query in the URL, not in useState. Shareable and back-button friendly.
Lift only when siblings need it — not before
In an interview say "first colocation, then composition, finally memo" — that is the correct order
terms: keeping state next to where it is used
moving state up to the common parent
where: field-level state next to the field

t1-6.what:
Definition: Accessibility is not added later — it is built into the component's design. Four things are required in every widget:

  1. Semantic HTML — <button>, <nav>, <dialog> (not onClick on a div)
  2. Keyboard — Tab, Enter/Space, Arrow, Escape, Home/End
  3. ARIA — role, state (aria-expanded), relationship (aria-controls)
  4. Focus management — where it should go when opened, and where it should return when closed
t1-6.why:
Mentioning a11y in an interview is a signal of seniority — few people do it. And practically: <div onClick> cannot be clicked with the keyboard, the screen reader does not read it, and the Enter key does not work. <button> provides all three for free.

The best rule: choose the correct HTML element first. Half of accessibility is achieved there. Apply ARIA only when the needed element does not exist in HTML (tabs, combobox).
pros: Half the work is free with Semantic HTML
Keyboard users, screen reader users, and power users all benefit
You stand out immediately in an interview
cons: Testing requires a real screen reader (NVDA/VoiceOver)
Applying ARIA incorrectly is worse than not applying it
Focus management has many edge cases
gotchas: ARIA's first rule: no ARIA > incorrect ARIA. Choose the correct HTML element first.
aria-label overrides native text — the screen reader will read that, not the visible text
Never remove the focus outline — style it with :focus-visible, don't set display to none
terms: Accessible Rich Internet Applications — extra information for screen readers
only one element in a group is tab-focusable, the rest are reachable via arrow keys
keep focus confined inside a modal
where: mentioning a11y is a signal of seniority
WCAG is mandatory in large companies

t2-1.what:
Definition: 10,000 rows of DOM kill the browser. In virtualization only ~20 visible rows get DOM; the scrollbar's height is faked with a spacer.

In a design round this is the standard answer for a "large list" — but saying it alone isn't enough, you have to state its tradeoffs.
t2-1.why:
Each DOM node has memory and layout cost. 10k rows cause the browser to freeze for 5-10 seconds. In a virtualized list, only 20 nodes remain, so 10k and 1 M rows run at roughly the same speed.

But in an interview say — virtualization is not free: Ctrl+F doesn’t work, content isn’t visible to SEO, and variable-height rows require measurement. Therefore, don’t apply it for up to 200 rows.
pros: Performance is almost independent of list size
Memory usage is very low
Scrolling stays smooth even with 1 M rows
cons: Browser find-in-page and SEO both stop working
Scroll can jump with variable-height rows
Accessibility (screen readers don’t see the full list) requires extra work
gotchas: In an interview, mentioning tradeoffs is essential — just saying "we’ll virtualize" sounds junior
If estimateSize is wrong for variable height, the scrollbar jumps — use measureElement
Don’t virtualize up to 200 rows — a plain list works fine
terms: rendering only the visible items in the DOM
extra rows just outside the window to keep scrolling smooth
each row has a different height — the hardest case

t2-2.what:
Definition: Three ways to show large datasets — numbered pagination, infinite scroll, and load more button. And on the backend there are two approaches — offset or cursor.

In the design round both decisions are separate and both are asked.
t2-2.why:
Offset bug that appears in every interview: you are viewing page 1, a new item gets added at the top. Now you request page 2 — the item that was at the end of page 1 slides down and appears at the top of page 2. You will see it again. If an item is deleted, one item will be skipped.

This does not happen with a cursor because you send an identifier, not a position — "the items after this id". Therefore every real-time feed (Twitter, Slack) uses a cursor.
pros: Cursor: consistent results, fast on the DB (index seek, no OFFSET scan)
Numbered: user can jump, shareable URL, back button works
Load more: benefits of infinite scroll plus accessible footer
cons: Cursor: "go to page 5" not possible
Infinite scroll: scroll position is lost on back button, footer not reachable
Offset: DB slow on large offsets (OFFSET 100000 = scanning 100k rows)
gotchas: Offset drift bug is a favorite interview question — have a duplicate/skip example ready
In infinite scroll, handle scroll restoration yourself — otherwise the back button takes the user to the top
Don’t use a scroll listener, use IntersectionObserver — scroll events fire up to 60 times per second
terms: items repeat or get skipped when a new item arrives
where: numbered pagination (user needs to go to page 5)
Load more button — footer also available

t2-3.what:
Definition: Data table design round is classic because it includes everything — sorting, filtering, pagination, virtualization, column resize, row selection, sticky header, and responsive.

The most important decision: server-side or client-side? Up to 1,000 rows client, above that server.
t2-3.why:
In interviews, people jump straight into implementation. The right approach: first ask about the scale — "how many rows? 100 or 1,000,000?" Based on that the entire architecture changes:

  • <1,000 rows — everything on client, sort/filter in memory, no API
  • >1,000 — server-side sorting/filtering/pagination, client only displays
  • >10,000 visible — also add virtualization

Server-side removes dataset size limit

Tables are inherently poor on mobile — a different layout is needed
gotchas: First ask "how many rows?" — the entire design depends on it
Track row selection by id, not by index — index changes after sorting
Implement sticky header with CSS (position:sticky), not with a JS scroll listener

t2-4.what:
Definition: Every data-driven UI has four states, not three:

  1. Loading — skeleton (not a spinner, if the shape is known)
  2. Error — what happened + retry button
  3. Empty — two separate: "there was never any data" vs "nothing found with the filter"
  4. Success — actual content

Calling out these four in a design round shows maturity — a junior only thinks about loading and success.
t2-4.why:
An empty state should have two forms because the user's need differs. "No orders yet" → they need a button to start shopping. "This filter found nothing" → they need a button to clear the filter. Showing a single "No data" is useless in both cases.

And a skeleton is better than a spinner because it reserves the layout — the page doesn't jump when the content arrives (CLS = 0).
pros: Skeleton gives CLS zero — page doesn’t jump
Correct empty state tells the user the next step
Retry button lets a transient network error self-heal
cons: Four states = four UI pieces to build + maintain
Skeleton must be kept in sync with content
Too many skeletons make the page feel "busy"
gotchas: Create two separate empty states — “never had data” and “not found with filter” are completely different
Keep the skeleton’s height the same as a real row, otherwise the page will shift when content appears
Always provide a retry in the error state — without retry the error state is a dead end
terms: grey placeholder matching the shape of the content
UI for when there is no data at all
Cumulative Layout Shift — page jumping when content arrives
where: each widget has its own four states

t2-5.what:
Definition: In an optimistic update you assume that the server will say yes — you update the UI immediately, then send the request in the background. If it fails, revert to the previous state.

Three things are required: (1) save the previous state, (2) rollback on failure, (3) later reconcile with the server.
t2-5.analogy: Ask a friend for ₹100. You assume they will give it and make a plan. If they refuse, cancel the plan — but by then you saved time.
t2-5.why:
The Like button shows a 300 ms wait. With optimistic updates the app feels "instant" — this is the biggest lever for perceived performance.

But not every action should be optimistic. In an interview say: "optimistic only when the chance of failure is low and rollback is cheap." Like, star, reorder — yes. Payment, delete, checkout — never.
pros: App feels instant — the biggest lever for perceived performance
Huge difference on slow networks
First step toward offline-first
cons: Rollback logic must be written for every mutation
Race conditions on rapid clicking
User may see an incorrect state (briefly)
gotchas: In onMutate, always cancelQueries — otherwise an old in-flight response will erase your optimistic update
Never make irreversible actions (payment, delete) optimistic
Show a toast with the rollback — silently reverting confuses the user
terms: changing the UI before the server responds
restoring the previous state when the server fails
sending the same request twice still has the same effect

t2-6.what:
Definition: API provides nested data — each post contains the full author object. If the same author has 20 posts, that object is in memory 20 times. If the author's name changes, you have to change it in 20 places.

In normalization you flatten the data — { posts: {id: post}, users: {id: user} } — and keep only authorId in the post.
t2-6.analogy: Writing the full address in every row in Excel vs creating a separate "customers" sheet and storing only the customer ID. If the address changes, update it in one place, not in 500 rows.
t2-6.why:
This comes up in interviews when an entity appears in multiple places — the user's name on every chat message, the author on every feed post. Without normalization, a single update can leave half the UI stale.

But it is not required everywhere. With caches like React Query, a simple invalidate is often sufficient. Use normalization when: the entity appears in multiple places, you need real-time updates, or you need offline support.

Lower memory (no duplicate objects)
Applying real-time patches becomes trivial

Boilerplate — need to write both normalize and denormalize
Completely overkill for small apps
gotchas: Don't normalize everywhere — React Query's invalidate often suffices
Keep order separate (feed: string[]) — don't rely on object key order
You can use a library like Normalizr, but a 30-line custom function is usually enough

t3-1.what:
Definition: Both reduce rapid events, but the approach is different:

  • Debounce — "do nothing until it stops". For search input.
  • Throttle — "keep going, but only once every 200ms". For scroll, resize, mouse-move.

Search box needs debounce because sending an API call on every keystroke wastes money and exhausts rate limits.
t3-1.analogy: Elevator door. Debounce = if someone is coming, wait; close only when no one arrives for 3 seconds. Throttle = it will close once every 10 seconds, regardless of how many people arrive.
t3-1.why:
In a design round, saying only "we’ll add debounce" is a half answer. The complete answer has three parts:

  1. Debounce — reduces network calls (typical 300ms)
  2. Cancel/abort — stop the previous in-flight request, otherwise an out-of-order response will show stale results
  3. Cache — if the same query comes again, don’t hit the network

Debounce alone does not eliminate a race condition — that is a separate problem.
pros: Network calls reduced 10–20×
Both rate limit and server load are saved
Abort eliminates the out-of-order results bug
cons: Debounce increases perceived latency (an extra 300ms)
Wrong delay makes the UI either laggy or spammy
Debounce alone does not fix a race condition
gotchas: Debounce + abort + cache — mention all three; saying only debounce is a half answer
Keep the debounced function in useMemo/useRef otherwise a new timer is created on every render
Don’t apply debounce on scroll — use throttle there, otherwise nothing will happen during scrolling
terms: wait for it to stop — invoke after N ms from the last event
rate limit — at most once every N ms
run at the end of the window or at the start

t3-2.what:
Definition: The most common question in an autocomplete design round because it includes everything — debounce, caching, race conditions, keyboard navigation, ARIA, virtualization, and highlighting.

The complete answer consists of 5 layers: input handling → network → cache → keyboard/ARIA → rendering.
t3-2.why:
The interviewer checks how many layers you remember. Most people stop after mentioning debounce + fetch. Those who also mention these stand out:

  • Keyboard: Arrow up/down, Enter, Escape, Home/End
  • ARIA: role="combobox", aria-expanded, aria-activedescendant — stays focused on the input
  • Minimum length (2 chars), and empty/no-results state
  • Highlight — matched portion bold, and escape user input (XSS)
pros: Instant response when typing the same query again thanks to cache
Keyboard navigation means power users don’t need a mouse
Minimum length prevents unnecessary API calls
cons: Many edge cases — blur, click, escape, IME input
On mobile, competition for space between keyboard and dropdown
If results exceed 1,000, virtualization is also needed

t3-3.what:
Definition: Large form architecture has three decisions:

  1. Where state — controlled (render on every keystroke) or uncontrolled (via RHF, refs)
  2. When to validate — onChange / onBlur / onSubmit, and where the schema lives
  3. How to show errors — below the field, summary on top, or both

Design round answer: uncontrolled + schema validation + onBlur first, onChange after first error.
t3-3.why:
30 fields controlled = 30 components render on every keystroke. RHF keeps it uncontrolled, so typing causes zero re-renders — only renders when an error appears.

Validation timing is a big part of UX: don’t start with onChange — the user will type “m” and see “invalid email”, which is irritating. Correct pattern: first validate on onBlur; once an error appears, validate on onChange so the error disappears as soon as it’s corrected.

Type + validation from a single source with schema
You can map server errors to fields
cons: Need to wrap custom components (MUI, Radix) with Controller
Cross-field validation (password match) requires a bit extra work
Async validation (username available?) can have race conditions
gotchas: Don’t start validation with onChange — start with onTouched (blur), then onChange
Provide defaultValues or you’ll get an “uncontrolled to controlled” warning
Connect the error to the input with aria-describedby, otherwise screen readers won’t know about the error

t3-4.what:
Definition: Keyboard navigation design means that every interaction can happen without a mouse. Four questions for each widget:

  1. Where does focus go when the widget opens?
  2. Which keys do what? (Arrow, Enter, Escape, Tab)
  3. Where does focus return when it closes?
  4. Is focus trapped (modal) or free (dropdown)?
t3-4.why:
This is not just accessibility — power users also use the keyboard. Gmail, Linear, Slack are all keyboard-first and that is their competitive advantage.

In the design round, when you say "close with Escape, return focus to the trigger", the interviewer sees that you built a real production component.
pros: Power users get a very fast workflow

t4-1.what:
Definition: Three ways to bring real-time data:

  • Polling — the client asks repeatedly. Simple, but latency equals the interval, and wasteful requests.
  • SSE — server pushes, one direction. Runs over HTTP, auto-reconnect built-in.
  • WebSocket — two-way, full duplex. Most powerful, requires the most infrastructure work.
t4-1.why:
In an interview, don’t say WebSocket by default — that’s a junior signal. The correct answer comes from the requirements:

  • If the client needs to send (chat, cursor, collaboration)? → WebSocket
  • If it only needs to receive (notifications, live scores, AI token stream)? → SSE — simple, cheap, auto-reconnect
  • If updates are rare (every 30 seconds)? → polling — do nothing else

The big point about SSE: it uses normal HTTP, so proxy/CDN/auth work without extra configuration.

t4-2.what:
Definition: Connection will break — WiFi changed, tunnel arrived, laptop slept, server deployed. The question is not whether it will break, the question is how it will reconnect.

Four things are needed: (1) exponential backoff + jitter, (2) fill the gap of missed messages, (3) offline queue, (4) show the user the connection status.
t4-2.why:
Thundering herd is the core of this topic. The server was down for 30 seconds. It came back. Now 50,000 clients will reconnect at once and the server will crash again. Jitter is the remedy — if each client waits a random time, the load is spread.

In an interview, say "exponential backoff with jitter" — it is much better than just saying backoff.
pros: Jitter prevents the server reconnect storm.
Offline queue ensures the user's message is not lost.
Since/Last-Event-ID fills missed messages.
cons: It requires managing a lot of state.
Filling the gap needs server-side message history.
Testing is difficult (you have to simulate the network).

Show the user the connection status (live / reconnecting / offline) — silently failing is the worst UX.

t4-3.what:
Definition: As soon as a message is sent in the chat, it should appear on the screen — no waiting for server confirmation. For this you need:

  2. When the server response arrives, replace the temp id with the real id
  3. If it fails, set status failed + retry button — do not delete the message
t4-3.why:
This differs from a normal optimistic update because there is an identity problem — the client creates an id, the server creates its own, and the same message can arrive again via WebSocket (echo). Without a temp-id mapping, a duplicate will appear.

And when it fails, the message should not be removed — the user typed it, that's effort. A failed state + retry is the correct UX.

t4-4.what:
Definition: Presence (online/offline) and typing indicators are ephemeral data — they are not saved in the DB, they only reside in memory/Redis with a short TTL.

Two standard patterns: presence via heartbeat + TTL, typing via throttled event + auto-expire.
t4-4.why:
A naive typing indicator sends an event on every keystroke — 60 messages per minute per user. In a room with 50 people this becomes 3,000 messages/minute just for "typing". The correct approach: throttle (one "typing" event every 3 seconds) and on the receiver side use auto-expire (remove it automatically after 5 seconds).

Auto-expire is necessary because a "stopped typing" event can be lost (e.g., the user disconnects, network drops) — then the indicator would remain stuck forever.

t4-6.what:
Definition: What happens if two people change the same thing at the same time? Three strategies:

  • LWW — the one with the later timestamp wins. Simple. The other's work disappears silently.
  • OT — transform each operation according to the other’s. Powerful, but requires a central server and is very hard to implement.
  • CRDT — design a data structure so that merges always produce the same result. No server needed, but uses more memory.
t4-6.analogy: Two people are writing in the same Google Doc. LWW = the version whose save happened later is kept, the other's is lost. CRDT = both people's words stay in their own places, nothing is lost.
t4-6.why:
In an interview there is no expectation that you will implement CRDT yourself. The expectation is that you:

  1. Identify the conflict — "what if two people edit at the same time?"
  2. Choose the right strategy for the product — LWW is fine for a form field, not for a text editor
  3. Know the library name — Yjs (CRDT), Automerge

And a practical fallback: field-level locking — "Riya is editing this field" — sufficient for many business apps and takes one day to build.

Version check: easy to implement and data never disappears silently
Field locking: the simplest and clearly visible to the user
cons: CRDT: memory overhead and heavy mental model

LWW: data disappears silently — the user doesn't even notice
gotchas: Don't implement CRDT yourself — use Yjs or Automerge, and say that in the interview
Use a server timestamp for LWW, not the client’s — client clocks are inaccurate
Silent overwrite is the worst option — showing a conflict dialog on a 409 response is sufficient

Conflict-free Replicated Data Type — data that merges automatically

t5-1.what:
Definition: The four decisions of SPA routing architecture:

  1. Code splitting — each route gets its own chunk (lazy + Suspense)
  2. Data loading — from a loader before render, or inside the component
  3. Nested layouts — no re-render when navigating the sidebar/nav
  4. Prefetch — load the next route on hover/viewport
t5-1.why:
The core interview point is the waterfall. The old pattern: route match → chunk download → component render → useEffect → data fetch. These are three sequential steps — 300ms + 200ms + 400ms.

In loader-based routing, the router knows which data is required as soon as the route matches, so chunks and data run in parallel. And in nested routes, all matching loaders run together, not one after another.

State in a nested layout is preserved when navigating
Prefetch makes navigation feel instant
cons: If you split too much, each navigation triggers a new request
You need to learn the loader mental model
Hooks cannot be used inside a data loader
gotchas: Use Promise.all in the loader — sequential await brings the waterfall back
Prefetch on hover — on mobile you need to use touchstart (hover never occurs)
Route-level splitting is the biggest win — don’t start with component-level splitting

t5-2.what:
Definition: "State management" is not a single thing, there are four separate things — and each has its own tool:

  1. Server state → React Query / SWR / RTK Query
  2. URL state → searchParams
  3. Global client state → Zustand / Jotai / Context
  4. Local state → useState / useReducer

In the design round, mentioning these four is the real answer — not "I'll use Redux".
t5-2.why:
90% of the "pain of state management" comes from treating server state like client state. Server data needs caching, refetching, deduplication, stale detection — Redux provides none of this, so people write it manually and the store grows to 5,000 lines.

Separate server state, separate URL state — the remaining global client state is often so small that a 30-line Zustand store is enough.

Each tool is best at its own job
URL state provides free shareability

Don't copy server data into the store — you'll end up with two sources of truth
Context is not a state manager — it's a dependency injection tool

t5-3.what:
Definition: the three parts of frontend auth:

  1. Where to store the token — httpOnly cookie (safe) vs localStorage (gets stolen in XSS)
  2. How to refresh — on a 401, only one refresh runs, and all pending requests wait for it
  3. Authorization — what to show (UI) and what to allow (server)
t5-3.why:
The most important line to say in an interview: frontend authorization is only UX, not security. Hiding a button does not make any API safe — a user can send a request from DevTools. The real check is always on the server.

And token storage: a token in localStorage gets stolen via XSS. An httpOnly cookie cannot be read by JavaScript — but for CSRF you need SameSite=Strict or a CSRF token. Mentioning this tradeoff is essential.

Single-flight refresh prevents a refresh storm
Cross-tab logout keeps security consistent
cons: CSRF protection is needed separately when using cookies
Refresh logic has many edge cases (what if the refresh itself returns 401?)
Keeping permissions on the client increases payload size

t5-6.what:
Definition: i18n is not just about translating strings. There are five parts:

  1. Strings — keys + translation files, lazy load per locale
  2. Plurals & gender — ICU format (each language has different rules)
  3. Formatting — date, number, currency (Intl API)
  4. RTL — layout mirroring for Arabic/Hebrew
  5. Locale detection — URL, cookie, or Accept-Language
t5-6.why:
Most common mistake: string concatenation. "You have " + n + " items" cannot be translated because each language has a different word order, and plural rules differ — Russian has four plural forms, Arabic has six. That’s why ICU format exists.

Another mistake: putting all language translations in a single bundle. 20 languages × 50 KB = 1 MB, but the user only uses 50 KB. Perform locale-wise lazy load.

ICU provides correct plural/gender handling for every language
Logical CSS properties make RTL almost free
cons: Translation workflow (TMS, translators) has its own process
Text expansion — German can be 30% longer, causing layout breakage
Testing must be done for every locale
gotchas: Never concatenate strings — use ICU message format

Prepare the layout for text expansion — German/Finnish text can be 30–40% longer
